title: Smooth ganache coat
subtitle: achieving a sharp, mirror-smooth finish with chocolate ganache
excerpt: Coating a cake in ganache produces a firmer, more stable surface than buttercream and gives sharp edges that hold at room temperature. The technique requires a crumb coat with chilling, then a final pour or spread of ganache at the right temperature, followed by scraping and chilling again. It is the standard base coat for fondant-covered showpiece cakes and works as a finished coat in its own right.
sourceNotes: Ganache as a cake coating is a classical French patisserie technique dating to the 19th century. The term ganache refers to the emulsion of cream and chocolate; its use as a coating layer beneath fondant or as a smooth finished coat became standard in professional cake decorating from the mid-20th century onward and is taught in all professional patisserie programmes.

recipe.yieldDescription: enough to coat and crumb-coat one 20 cm round layer cake
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make ganache the day before. Store covered at room temperature in cool weather, or refrigerate and warm gently before use.

glossaryTerms.definition: An emulsion of chocolate and cream. The ratio of cream to chocolate determines the texture: equal parts by weight gives a pourable ganache; a 1:2 ratio (cream:chocolate) gives a firm, spreadable consistency suitable for coating cakes.

A thin preliminary coat of ganache or buttercream applied over the whole cake to seal in loose crumbs. Once chilled firm, a second full coat can be applied cleanly without crumbs contaminating the surface.

content.text: coat requires working in two stages separated by a chill: a

to seal the cake, then a final coat scraped smooth. The ganache temperature at each stage matters: too warm and it runs off; too cold and it tears when scraped. A bench scraper and turntable are not optional here.

For a coating ganache, use a 1:2 ratio of double cream to dark chocolate by weight (e.g., 150 ml cream to 300 g chocolate). Bring the cream to a simmer, pour over finely chopped chocolate in a bowl, and leave for 2 minutes. Stir from the centre outward with a spatula until completely smooth and glossy. Cool to a spreadable consistency, around 27 to 28°C for dark chocolate ganache: it should hold a soft peak when a spatula is lifted from the bowl.

Place the chilled, filled cake on the turntable. Apply a thin layer of ganache over the top and sides using a palette knife, spreading it as evenly as you can but not worrying about perfection. The aim is to seal all surfaces. Use the bench scraper held at a 90° angle against the side and spin the turntable to remove excess and leave a rough but even coat. Refrigerate for 30 to 45 minutes until the crumb coat is completely firm.

Check the ganache consistency again before the final coat. If it has set too firm, warm the bowl briefly over hot water and stir until spreadable. Apply a generous layer to the top of the cake first, spreading it level with a palette knife. Then apply to the sides, building up a slightly thicker coat than you want in the final result. Hold the bench scraper at a 90° angle to the side, press it lightly against the ganache, and spin the turntable in one smooth, continuous motion. The excess ganache curls off the scraper; use it to fill any thin patches.

After scraping the sides, a small ridge of ganache will sit at the top edge. Hold the palette knife flat and draw it inward across the top of the cake from the outer edge toward the centre, working in short passes. This pushes the overhanging edge back down and sharpens the corner. Refrigerate for 30 minutes. To achieve an extremely sharp edge, dip the palette knife in hot water, dry it, and run it once along the top edge just before final chilling.

attrs.problem: Ganache tears when scraped rather than spreading smooth

content.text: The ganache was too cold. Warm slightly and allow to soften until a spatula leaves an impression but the ganache still holds its shape.

attrs.problem: Bubbles or pits in the final coat

content.text: Bubbles form when ganache is stirred vigorously. For the final coat, stir very gently and avoid folding in air. Press a small palette knife over any pits after chilling: warm the metal with your hand and press flat to smooth them.
